planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees spring through fall; Yates is a small-fruited 19th-century Southern heirloom apple valued for exceptional disease resistance, reliable annual bearing, and outstanding storage life, making it one of the most trouble-free apples for Deep South orchards.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Yates is a Georgia heirloom apple dating to the early-to-mid 1800s, prized by Southern orchardists for its outstanding resistance to fire blight, cedar-apple rust, and other diseases that plague apple growing in the humid South, along with dependable annual production even in years when other varieties bear poorly. The fruit is small, red-striped over yellow, with firm, crisp, tart-sweet flesh better suited to cider, preserves, and cooking than fresh eating, though many old-time growers enjoy it fresh once it mellows in storage. Its most celebrated trait is exceptional keeping quality — properly stored fruit holds firm and flavorful for months longer than most apples, historically making it a reliable source of fresh fruit through winter before refrigeration was common. Because it requires a moderate chill accumulation, it performs best in zone 6-8 and is marginal in the mildest parts of zone 9. Plant with another apple variety for cross-pollination, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good air circulation and disease prevention.

common_name: Carolina Red June Apple (Early-Ripening Southern Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees spring through fall; Carolina Red June is one of the earliest-ripening Southern heirloom apples, producing small, deep red fruit as early as June, well ahead of most apple varieties, with low chill requirements suited to the warmer parts of the South.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Carolina Red June is a Southern heirloom apple documented since at least the early 1800s and grown widely across the antebellum South, valued above all for its extremely early ripening, often ready to pick in June, weeks ahead of nearly every other apple variety and giving Southern growers fresh apples at a time of year when no other apple is available. Fruit is small to medium, deep red over a yellow background, with crisp, juicy, mildly tart flesh good for fresh eating, sauce, and early-season pies. Trees are vigorous and productive, and the variety's relatively low chill requirement makes it one of the more Gulf-South-adapted heirloom apples compared with higher-chill Northern varieties. Because it ripens so early and doesn't store particularly long, plan to use or process the crop promptly rather than relying on it for winter storage. Plant with another apple variety nearby for cross-pollination, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good air circulation.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Carolina Red June Apple heirloom notes
North Carolina State University — Old Southern Apple Cultivars

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees spring through fall; King David is an 1893 Arkansas heirloom apple, likely a chance seedling of Jonathan and Winesap, known for a rich, wine-like flavor and better disease resistance than many of its high-chill Northern contemporaries.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun. King David originated as a chance seedling discovered on an Arkansas farm in 1893, believed to be a natural cross of Jonathan and Winesap, and quickly gained a following for its rich, aromatic, distinctly wine-like flavor that many heirloom apple enthusiasts still rank among the best-tasting of the old Southern apples. Fruit is medium-sized, deep red over a yellow background, with firm, crisp, juicy flesh that holds up well for fresh eating, baking, and cider. Trees show good vigor and better resistance to common apple diseases than many high-chill Northern varieties of the same era, though it still needs a moderate winter chill and performs best in zone 5-8, becoming marginal in the mildest parts of zone 9. Plant with another apple variety for cross-pollination, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open, well-ventilated canopy that reduces disease pressure in humid climates.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees spring through fall; Shockley is a small-fruited Georgia heirloom apple from the early 1800s celebrated for extraordinarily long storage life, historically keeping in a root cellar into the following spring without refrigeration.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Shockley is a Georgia heirloom apple dating to the early 1800s, once one of the most widely planted commercial apples in the South before refrigerated shipping and storage made its greatest strength less essential: fruit stored in a cool root cellar could reportedly keep in good eating condition into the following spring, an almost unmatched keeping quality among apples of any era. Fruit is small, yellow with a red blush, firm and crisp with a mildly sweet, slightly tart flavor that some describe as unremarkable fresh off the tree but that mellows and improves markedly in storage, developing a richer, more complex flavor over weeks and months. Trees are vigorous, productive, and relatively disease-resistant for an older Southern heirloom, ripening late in the season. Plant with another apple variety nearby for cross-pollination, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good air circulation and disease prevention in humid climates.

common_name: Maxine Pear (Starking Delicious Fire Blight-Resistant Southern Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Maxine, also sold as Starking Delicious, is a large-fruited fire blight-resistant pear developed for Southern growing conditions, similar in use and reliability to Moonglow and Orient.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Maxine cross-pollinates well with Moonglow, Orient, Kieffer, and most other fire blight-resistant Southern pear varieties. Maxine, also marketed as Starking Delicious, was developed for good disease resistance and reliable production in the humid Southeast, where fire blight quickly kills susceptible European pear varieties like Bartlett. It produces large, smooth, yellow-green fruit with sweet, juicy, only lightly gritty flesh, notably larger than many of its fire-blight-resistant peers, ripening in late summer. Like most Southern-adapted pears, it should be picked while still firm and green and ripened off the tree in a cool spot for the best texture and flavor, since fruit left to ripen on the tree tends to soften unevenly from the core outward. Trees are vigorous and productive, and the strong disease resistance means Maxine needs little to no fungicide spraying to produce a reliable crop in Gulf South conditions. Plant with another European pear variety for best cross-pollination and yield.
sources: Virginia Cooperative Extension — Fruit Culture Guide: Fire Blight-Resistant Pears
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pear Variety Selection for Texas
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Pear Cultivars for the Gulf South
